agency_full: National Aeronautics and Space Administration / Jet Propulsion Laboratory
payload: Planetary flyby spacecraft; three RTG modules totalling ~470 W at launch (decaying to ~250 W today)
credit: © NASA / JPL-Caltech — U.S. Government work, public domain. Voyager 1 is the most distant human-made object — about 170 AU from the Sun and travelling at ~17 km/s relative to it. Saturn is the catalogued destination because Voyager 1's mission profile ended there; its Titan flyby (1980-11-12) bent the trajectory upward out of the ecliptic plane, and after that no further planetary encounter was possible. The spacecraft crossed the heliopause on 2012-08-25 — the first human-made object to enter interstellar space. Pale Blue Dot family photograph taken 1990-02-14 from a heliocentric distance of ~6 billion km. Mission planning credit: Gary Flandro, JPL, who identified the late-1970s outer-planet alignment that made the Grand Tour possible.

events.label: Launch — Titan IIIE / Centaur
events.description: Cape Canaveral, 1977-09-05. Launched 16 days AFTER Voyager 2 but on a higher-energy direct trajectory that overtakes its twin en route to Jupiter. Gary Flandro's Grand Tour mission profile exploits a late-1970s outer-planet alignment that won't recur for ~175 years; the chemical engine alone can't reach Saturn, so Jupiter's gravity does the bending.

events.label: Jupiter — gravity assist
events.description: Closest approach 348,890 km from the cloud tops on 1979-03-05. The encounter discovers Jupiter's rings, captures Io's active volcanism (Linda Morabito's chance pixel), and maps the magnetic-field structure that traps the Io plasma torus. Jupiter's gravity slingshots Voyager 1 to ~17 km/s heliocentric, set up for Titan's haze at Saturn 21 months later.

events.label: Saturn — flyby + Titan probe
events.description: Closest approach 124,000 km from Saturn on 1980-11-12; the prior day Voyager 1 passes within 6500 km of Titan to probe its nitrogen haze. The Titan-targeted geometry bends the trajectory 35° upward out of the ecliptic plane, ending any future planetary encounter — Voyager 1 is now committed to interstellar space. Heliopause crossing followed on 2012-08-25; the spacecraft is the most distant human-made object.
